I eventually inherited a Blue & White G3 and souped up that bad boy with 1GB of RAM, a huge hard disk, a super drive, and even slapped in an AGP graphics card. I ran 10.3 and 10.4 on that guy.

Later, I leapfrogged the G4 and got a lower-end G5 tower, again souped up, and used it to play WoW for a couple of years.

I also owned a 17" PowerBook G4 with 128MB of RAM, huge hard disk, maxxed out RAM. Ran 10.5 and dual boot with Classic. I used it until 2011 when the vertical line issue made it unusable.

I eventually replaced the G5 with an Early 2009 Mac Mini. Souped up as usual over the years. My first Intel Mac. It was a beast!

I then moved on to an Early 2011 MacBook Pro. Souped up with 8GB of ram. 500GB hard disk. It was a powerhouse. So much so, I decided I no longer wanted a desktop. That also meant I had to give up classic, which was fine. This MacBook Pro was plenty for me.

And then came this fall... as my MacBook Pro started to show its age, I looked to all of Apple's Mac products to see if a worthy successor was available. To my horror, the systems had all pretty much stagnated with tech from 2012/2013 in them.

As someone who took pride in upgrading and souping up his Macs for 2 decades, this is not the Apple I knew.

Then there's the question of precedent. Do you believe all women should be able to kill abusive husbands? What if the abuse goes both ways (in 80% of cases it does, and it certainly seemed to here)? What if the evidence he actually abused her is flimsy, and based on her word (it's not in this case; guy was a fucking asshole)? Should men who are abused by their wives be able to do the same, or is the right of vigilante justice exclusively given to women? Do we set a number of times abuse has to have taken place before killing is justified? Is there a time limit between the most recent episode of abuse and the killing where it counts as self-defense (in this case, she went and got the knife after he had smashed her arm in the door, so she wasn't protecting herself from an immediate threat -- although she claims to be scared he would hit her again later)?

There's a lot of grey area, and that's why we have courts and juries to decide this, not one person who looks over a case file and issues a royal decree.

The court decided to acquit her of murder, but give her a suspended sentence (ie no jail time, just probation) for involuntary manslaughter, which is essentially a warning saying she should have sought legal avenues to her problems instead of killing him.
